meta.title: US presidential elections, 1788-2024
sources: Wikipedia: electoral college results, popular vote tables and per-election articles (candidates, parties, votes, electoral votes, turnout)

eras.label: The Founding Era
eras.blurb: Washington was elected unanimously twice, then the first party system emerged: Federalists against Democratic-Republicans, a contest the Virginia dynasty won so completely that by 1820 opposition had dissolved into the Era of Good Feelings. Electors, chosen mostly by state legislatures at first, each cast two votes until the 12th Amendment separated president from vice president.

eras.label: Jacksonian Democracy
eras.blurb: Property qualifications fell, turnout among white men soared toward 80%, and the modern mass party was invented. Jackson's Democrats faced the Whigs in a stable two-party contest fought over banks, tariffs and executive power, while slavery pressed ever harder against the system's seams.

eras.label: Civil War & Reconstruction
eras.blurb: The Whigs collapsed, the anti-slavery Republicans rose in a single decade, and Lincoln's 1860 victory on 39.8% of the vote triggered secession. Reconstruction elections brought Black male suffrage and ended with 1876, the most disputed election in American history.

eras.label: The Gilded Age
eras.blurb: Two evenly matched machines fought razor-thin national elections: three of five winners in this era lost or tied the popular vote margin within a point. The Populist revolt and the realigning 1896 contest between McKinley and Bryan broke the deadlock in the Republicans' favor.

eras.label: Progressive Era to Normalcy
eras.blurb: Republican dominance was interrupted only when Roosevelt's 1912 third-party run split the party and let Wilson in. Women won the vote nationwide in 1920, doubling the electorate at a stroke, and the twenties produced three Republican landslides on prosperity.

eras.label: The New Deal Order
eras.blurb: The Depression destroyed Republican hegemony in a single election. Roosevelt's coalition of the South, cities, labor and immigrants won four consecutive terms, redefined the federal government, and survived his death when Truman's 1948 upset confounded every poll.

eras.label: Cold War Consensus
eras.blurb: Eisenhower's landslides bracketed the closest election of the century in 1960, the first fought on television. The era closed with Johnson's record 61% and the Civil Rights Act, which began prying the South loose from the Democratic coalition.

eras.label: The Long Realignment
eras.blurb: Wallace's 46 electoral votes in 1968 signalled the New Deal coalition's fracture. Nixon and then Reagan converted the South and the white working class, producing three 49-state-scale landslides in five elections, while turnout drifted steadily downward.

eras.label: The Post-Cold-War Era
eras.blurb: Perot's 19% in 1992 was the strongest third-party vote since 1912, and no winner between 1992 and 2004 managed a popular majority above 51%. The era delivered the 2000 photo finish, decided by 537 votes in Florida and the Supreme Court.

eras.label: The Polarized Era
eras.blurb: Two coalitions of nearly equal size now meet in a handful of swing states: every election since 2012 has been decided by narrow margins in the same short list of battlegrounds. 2016 produced the fifth popular-vote/electoral-college split, 2020 the highest turnout since 1900, and 2024 the first Republican popular-vote win in twenty years.

elections.label: 1788–89
elections.summary: Washington was elected unanimously, the only president chosen without opposition, with Adams becoming vice president under the original two-votes-per-elector system. New York, North Carolina and Rhode Island cast no electoral votes, their ratification politics unresolved.

Washington was again unanimous, and the first party contest happened underneath him: Clinton's 50 electoral votes for vice president marked the emerging Democratic-Republican opposition to Hamilton's program.

The first contested presidential election produced a Federalist president and a Democratic-Republican vice president, Adams and Jefferson, an awkwardness the two-vote system made possible. Margin in the Electoral College: three votes.

Jefferson's victory over Adams was the first peaceful transfer of power between parties in modern history, but a tie with his own running mate Burr threw it into the House for 36 ballots. The 12th Amendment followed directly.
Running with the Louisiana Purchase behind him and the 12th Amendment now separating the offices, Jefferson swept 162 of 176 electoral votes against Pinckney.
Madison inherited Jefferson's coalition comfortably despite the deep unpopularity of the trade embargo, though the Federalists doubled their electoral vote.
The first wartime presidential election: Madison held off DeWitt Clinton, backed by an unusual fusion of Federalists and dissident Republicans, in the closest contest between 1800 and 1824.
Monroe crushed Rufus King in the last election the Federalists ever contested, their opposition to the war having destroyed them as a national force.

Monroe ran effectively unopposed at the height of the Era of Good Feelings, taking every electoral vote but one. The 16% recorded against him was cast for scattered Federalist electors with no candidate.

candidates.name: John Quincy Adams
candidates.vp: John C. Calhoun and Andrew Jackson

elections.summary: Four Democratic-Republicans split the vote; Jackson led in both popular votes and electors but short of a majority, and the House elected Adams after Clay threw him his support. Jackson's followers called it corrupt and spent four years building the first mass party in response.

Jackson's rematch against Adams, fought amid a hugely expanded franchise and unprecedented turnout, founded the Democratic Party as the world's first modern electoral machine. The campaign was also among the nastiest ever run.
Jackson won re-election on his war against the Second Bank of the United States, beating Clay decisively. It was the first election with national nominating conventions, an Anti-Masonic invention.

Van Buren, Jackson's designated heir, defeated a Whig strategy of running three regional candidates intended to throw the race to the House. Johnson's vice-presidency was decided by the Senate, the only time that has happened.

The Whigs beat Van Buren with image politics: log cabins, hard cider and 'Tippecanoe and Tyler Too', on turnout near 80%, the highest of the era. Harrison died a month into office, making Tyler's succession the first test of the vice-presidency.
Polk, the first dark-horse nominee, beat Clay narrowly on an explicit platform of annexing Texas and Oregon. The Liberty Party's 62,000 votes in New York arguably cost Clay the presidency.
Taylor, a Mexican War hero with no stated politics, won for the Whigs while Van Buren's Free Soil run took 10% and split the New York Democrats, previewing the coming sectional crisis.
Pierce buried Scott in the Whigs' last national campaign; the party, fatally split over the Compromise of 1850, dissolved within four years.

The new Republican Party's first campaign carried eleven free states behind Frémont, while Buchanan won on Southern solidity plus Pennsylvania. Fillmore's Know Nothings took a fifth of the vote, the high-water mark of organized nativism.

Lincoln won every free state and the presidency with 39.8% of the vote against a three-way opposition, and appeared on no ballot in ten Southern states. Secession began within six weeks of the result.

The first presidential election held during civil war anywhere: Lincoln, running as National Union with Democrat Johnson, beat McClellan after Atlanta's fall turned the campaign, winning the soldier vote overwhelmingly.
Grant's margin rested on newly enfranchised Black voters in the Reconstruction South; Seymour carried the white-line vote. 'Let us have peace' met organized Klan violence at the polls.

Grant routed Greeley, the strange Liberal Republican-Democratic fusion nominee, who died between the election and the electoral count, his votes scattering among four men. The only major-party nominee to die mid-election.

Tilden won the popular vote by three points and led 184-165 with twenty electoral votes disputed across three Southern states. An Electoral Commission awarded all twenty to Hayes by 8-7 party-line votes, and Reconstruction was ended in the bargain that made it stick.
Garfield's popular margin over Hancock was under two thousand votes nationally, the narrowest ever recorded, though the Electoral College was comfortable. He was assassinated within a year.

Cleveland became the first Democratic president since Buchanan in a campaign of personal scandal on both sides, decided by a thousand-vote margin in New York after a Blaine surrogate's 'rum, Romanism and rebellion' slur.
Harrison lost the popular vote to Cleveland but won the presidency on the tariff question and superior organization in the swing states, the third popular-vote inversion and the last until 2000.
Cleveland completed the only split-term comeback until Trump repeated it in 2024. Weaver's Populists carried five Western states with 8.5%, announcing the agrarian revolt.

McKinley's businesslike front-porch campaign, funded on an unprecedented scale by Mark Hanna, beat Bryan's whirlwind free-silver crusade. The realignment it sealed kept Republicans dominant for a generation.
The McKinley-Bryan rematch, now fought on empire and prosperity, produced a wider Republican win and made Theodore Roosevelt vice president. An assassin's bullet promoted him within a year.
Roosevelt, the first accidental president to win in his own right, took the largest popular margin yet recorded and promptly promised not to run again, a pledge he came to regret.
Taft, Roosevelt's chosen successor, dispatched Bryan's third and final campaign comfortably; the Great Commoner remains the only major-party nominee beaten three times.

Roosevelt, denied the Republican nomination, ran as a Progressive and outpolled Taft, the only time a third party has beaten a major party. The split handed Wilson 435 electoral votes on 41.8%, and Debs took 6% for the Socialists.
Wilson held on against Hughes by 23 electoral votes on 'He kept us out of war'; California's 13 votes, decided by under 4,000 ballots, settled it. Five months later America was at war.

Harding's 60.3% remains among the largest popular-vote shares ever, a repudiation of Wilsonian internationalism in the first election with nationwide women's suffrage and the first with radio-reported returns. Debs polled 900,000 votes from a federal prison cell.
Coolidge won easily over a Democratic Party that had needed 103 convention ballots to nominate Davis, while La Follette's Progressives took a sixth of the vote and Wisconsin.
Hoover's landslide over Al Smith, the first Catholic major-party nominee, cracked the Solid South for the Republicans while Smith's urban gains quietly prefigured the New Deal coalition.

With a quarter of the workforce unemployed, Roosevelt carried 42 of 48 states on a promise of a New Deal, ending the Republican era at a stroke. The 20th Amendment soon ended the four-month lame-duck wait his crisis transition made intolerable.

The most crushing Electoral College verdict of the two-party era, 523 to 8: Roosevelt lost only Maine and Vermont. The Literary Digest's confident Landon prediction killed the straw poll and made modern survey research.
Breaking the two-term tradition unchallenged since Washington, Roosevelt beat the businessman-outsider Willkie as war spread in Europe, on the argument that the crisis outweighed the custom.

A wartime election run with soldier ballots across the world's battlefields: an exhausted, visibly ill Roosevelt won a fourth term over Dewey, with Truman substituted for Wallace on the ticket in the convention's most consequential switch.

The great upset: written off by every poll and pundit, and with Dixiecrat and Progressive revolts stripping both wings of his party, Truman whistle-stopped to a clear win. The Chicago Tribune's premature headline became the era's icon.

Eisenhower's 'I Like Ike' campaign ended twenty years of Democratic rule, swept even parts of the South, and was the first sold through television spots. Nixon saved his place on the ticket with the Checkers speech.
The Eisenhower-Stevenson rematch widened the margin amid the Suez and Hungary crises; prosperity and the general's personal standing overrode a Democratic Congress.

Kennedy beat Nixon by 0.17% of the popular vote, the closest of the century, after the first televised debates reshaped the race. Catholic-Protestant tensions, the missile-gap claim and disputed counts in Illinois and Texas all marked it.

Johnson's 61% remains the highest popular share ever recorded. Goldwater's ideological insurgency carried only his home state and the Deep South, where the Civil Rights Act had transformed the map, a defeat that incubated the conservative movement.

Amid assassinations, riots and Vietnam, Nixon edged Humphrey by half a million votes while Wallace's segregationist campaign took five Southern states, the last third-party electoral votes won by campaigning. The Democratic convention in Chicago became a byword for party crisis.

Nixon's 49-state landslide over McGovern was built on the Southern strategy and Democratic disarray; the break-in at the Watergate five months before the election went almost unnoticed by the voters it would ultimately consume.

Carter, an outsider running on trust after Watergate, narrowly beat the unelected incumbent Ford, whose pardon of Nixon and 'no Soviet domination' debate stumble both cost him. The South returned briefly to the Democratic column.

Reagan's 'Are you better off than you were four years ago?' converted a close race into a 44-state sweep amid inflation, gas lines and the Iran hostage crisis, and brought a Republican Senate with it. Anderson's independent run took 6.6%.

Morning in America: Reagan carried 49 states and 525 electoral votes against Mondale, who had promised to raise taxes and carried only Minnesota and DC. Ferraro was the first woman on a major-party ticket.

Bush became the first sitting vice president elected since Van Buren, riding peace, prosperity and a brutal negative campaign against Dukakis. A faithless elector voted for Bentsen, the losing VP nominee.

Clinton's war-room campaign ('the economy, stupid') unseated Bush as Perot took 18.9%, the biggest third-party vote since 1912, though not a single electoral vote. The baby-boom generation took the presidency.

Clinton cruised past Dole in a campaign without great stakes, the first re-elected Democratic president since Roosevelt, while turnout fell below half the voting-age population for the first time since 1924.

Gore won the popular vote; Bush won the presidency by 537 votes in Florida after a 36-day recount fight that ended in Bush v. Gore. The fourth popular-vote inversion, and the making of the modern election-law wars.
Bush won the only Republican popular-vote majority between 1988 and 2024, on terrorism and turnout machinery; Ohio's 118,000-vote margin was the hinge. Kerry conceded a day after the polls closed.

Obama's coalition of the young, minorities and the college-educated delivered the first Black presidency and the biggest Democratic win since 1964, amid financial collapse. Turnout hit its highest mark in forty years.
Obama became the first president since Reagan to win a majority twice, holding the Midwestern battlegrounds against Romney as the electorate's diversity outpaced Republican modelling.

Trump lost the popular vote by nearly three million yet won 304 electoral votes by flipping Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin by a combined 78,000 votes, the fifth inversion and the biggest polling shock since 1948. Seven faithless electors scattered, a modern record.

The pandemic election: record mail voting drove turnout to 66% of eligible voters, the highest since 1900, and Biden rebuilt the blue wall while flipping Georgia and Arizona. The result was certified through an unprecedented wave of legal challenges and the January 6 attack on the Capitol.

Trump completed the only Cleveland-style comeback, winning the popular vote as well as all seven battlegrounds, the first Republican popular win since 2004. Harris, elevated late after Biden's withdrawal, was the shortest-notice major-party nominee of the modern era.
